params.prompt: Priya adds disability coverage for her twenty employees. A group plan differs from Rosa’s individual policy in predictable ways. The employer holds the master contract and often pays the premium. There is no individual medical underwriting; everyone in the class is covered. Benefits are a percentage of salary rather than a chosen dollar amount, with a monthly maximum. Coverage is usually nonoccupational and offsets Social Security and workers compensation. Definitions tend to be split: own occupation for two years, then any occupation. If the employer pays the premium, benefits are taxable. Coverage ends when employment ends, though some plans allow conversion.

Short-term disability replaces income during the first weeks of a disability. Typical plans pay sixty to seventy percent of weekly salary for thirteen to twenty-six weeks, sometimes fifty-two. The elimination period is short, often zero days for accidents and seven for sickness, so benefits begin almost at once. Many employers self-fund S T D because claims are frequent, small and predictable, hiring an insurer only to administer them. S T D usually dovetails with sick leave, beginning when paid sick days run out. For Priya’s bakery, S T D keeps a worker recovering from surgery on the payroll for the three months it takes to heal.

Long-term disability begins where S T D ends. The elimination period is ninety or one hundred eighty days, matched to the S T D benefit period so the two plans hand off without a gap. Benefits replace fifty to sixty-seven percent of salary up to a monthly cap, reduced by Social Security, workers compensation and other income, and continue to age sixty-five or the Social Security normal retirement age. The definition is usually split at twenty-four months. Pre-existing condition limits are common, for example excluding conditions treated in the three months before coverage if disability begins within the first twelve months. L T D is almost always insured rather than self-funded.

Priya’s head baker developed the recipes that built the business. If he is disabled, revenue falls and a replacement must be recruited and trained. Key employee disability income insurance pays the business a monthly benefit or lump sum while the key person is disabled. The business is the applicant, owner, premium payer and beneficiary; the key employee is the insured. The benefit funds a temporary replacement, covers lost profits and buys time. Premiums are not deductible, and benefits are received tax-free. The key person’s own disability income is a separate matter, handled by his personal or group coverage.

If Rosa, a sole proprietor, is disabled, her income stops but the shop rent, utilities, employee wages, insurance premiums and loan payments continue. A business overhead expense policy reimburses those actual fixed expenses while the owner is disabled, up to a monthly maximum, for a short benefit period of one or two years, after a short elimination period, often thirty days. It does not pay the owner’s own salary or lost profit; her personal disability policy does that. B O E premiums are tax-deductible as a business expense, and benefits are taxable, but the expenses they pay are deductible, which nets to little tax.

Priya and her partner agree in writing that if either is permanently disabled, the other will buy her share. A disability buyout policy funds that purchase. After a long elimination period, typically one or two years so that the disability is clearly permanent, the policy pays a lump sum or installments to the business or the healthy partner, who uses it to buy out the disabled owner. Premiums are not deductible and benefits are tax-free. The arrangement gives the disabled owner cash for her interest and gives the business a clean transfer, mirroring the life insurance funded buy-sell agreement.

Rosa paid Social Security taxes for twenty years, which earned her work credits. To qualify for Social Security disability insurance she must be insured: generally forty credits, with twenty earned in the ten years before disability, and fewer for younger workers. She must also meet the program’s definition. Social Security is funded by payroll taxes and administered federally, and its disability benefit is an earned benefit, not welfare. A separate program, Supplemental Security Income, serves disabled people with little work history and limited means. Most exam questions concern the insurance program.

Social Security pays only for total disability. The claimant must be unable to engage in any substantial gainful activity because of a medically determinable physical or mental impairment that has lasted or is expected to last at least twelve months or to result in death. Substantial gainful activity is measured by a monthly earnings threshold that is indexed each year. There are no partial or short-term benefits. Rosa, who could manage a store, would be denied even though her own-occupation policy pays. That gap is exactly what the social insurance supplement rider in Lesson thirty addresses.

Benefits begin after a five-month waiting period, so the first payment covers the sixth full month of disability. The monthly amount is the worker’s primary insurance amount, the same figure used for retirement at full retirement age, based on lifetime earnings. Eligible family members, a spouse caring for young children and dependent children, may receive additional benefits subject to a family maximum. After twenty-four months of disability benefits the worker qualifies for Medicare regardless of age. Benefits continue while the disability lasts, with periodic reviews and work incentives that let a recipient test returning to work.

Workers compensation is a state system. In Maryland nearly every employer must carry it, through a private insurer, the Chesapeake Employers’ Insurance Company or approved self-insurance. It covers employees for accidental injuries and occupational diseases arising out of and in the course of employment. It is no-fault: the worker need not prove the employer was negligent, and the employer is protected from most lawsuits by the exclusive remedy rule. Rosa, self-employed with no employees, is not covered unless she elects coverage; Priya’s twenty employees are. Independent contractors are generally excluded, which is why the classification matters.

Maryland workers compensation pays medical expenses for the work injury without dollar limits. It pays wage replacement: temporary total disability at two-thirds of the average weekly wage, up to a state maximum, while the worker recovers; temporary partial while working at reduced pay; permanent partial disability on a schedule for lasting impairments; and permanent total disability for the most serious injuries. It funds vocational rehabilitation and pays death benefits to dependents plus funeral expenses. Disputes go to the Maryland Workers’ Compensation Commission. Benefits are tax-free, and private disability policies offset them.

Think of the three systems as layers. Workers compensation pays first for job injuries, quickly and without fault. Social Security pays for total, long-lasting disability from any cause, after five months and a strict test. Private disability income fills the gaps: injuries off the job, disabilities that are partial or occupation-specific, the five-month wait and the years before Social Security decides. Group plans offset the government benefits; individual policies generally pay in full, with riders that coordinate. A producer who knows the public programs can show exactly which gap each private dollar covers.
